question: Moving from California to Texas: what happens to your life insurance?
dek: If you are moving from California to Texas, your life insurance policy almost always travels with you, but a change of address update, a beneficiary review, and a conversation about community property differences are worth doing before the moving truck pulls away.
answer: In almost every case, your life insurance policy follows you when you move from California to Texas. The coverage does not cancel or restart just because you cross state lines. What you do need to do is notify your insurer of your new address, review your beneficiary designations, and think carefully about how Texas community property law may affect your estate plan in ways that differ from California. Because I am licensed in both California and Texas, I can stay your agent through the move and help you work through those questions without handing you off to a stranger.

sections.h: Your policy moves with you, but you still need to make a few updates
p: A life insurance contract is a private agreement between you and an insurance company, and it is not issued by your state the way a driver license is. When you move from the Conejo Valley to, say, Austin or Houston, the policy you bought in California does not expire, lapse, or need to be replaced. The insurer simply needs your new mailing address so that statements, renewal notices, and any correspondence reach you. That part is straightforward, and it usually takes one phone call or a quick form.

What catches people off guard is the beneficiary question. I see this come up a lot through my wife's work in probate real estate. A big move is exactly the kind of life event that makes people rethink who is named on the policy. Maybe a parent who was named years ago has since passed. Maybe you now have kids. Maybe the person you named lives back in Thousand Oaks and you want someone closer to your new life to have that responsibility. This is a good moment to pull out the policy and read who you have named as primary and contingent beneficiary, and to change it if something looks off.

sections.h: Community property: California and Texas are both community property states, but the details differ
p: Here is something that surprises a lot of people making this move. Both California and Texas are community property states, so the basic concept, that assets acquired during a marriage generally belong equally to both spouses, applies in both places. But the two states handle certain details differently, including how community property intersects with life insurance ownership, proceeds, and estate planning. I am a licensed agent, not an attorney, and this is exactly the kind of question you should raise with an estate planning lawyer who knows both states, ideally before you finalize the move.

What I can tell you from watching my wife work through probate cases is that when community property rules interact with a life insurance beneficiary designation in unexpected ways, it can slow down or complicate what gets to your family. The death benefit itself usually passes outside of probate directly to the named beneficiary, which is one of the strongest reasons to keep your beneficiary designations current. But the ownership of the policy, who pays the premiums, and how the policy is classified can all carry legal weight that varies by state. Get that conversation on the calendar with an attorney.

sections.h: Why being licensed in both states matters for Conejo Valley families on the move
p: I am based in Newbury Park and I hold a California license (4247326) and a Texas license (3268220). I added the Texas license specifically because I kept running into clients from the Conejo Valley and broader Ventura County area who were relocating to Texas and did not want to start over with an agent who did not know their history or their family situation. Life insurance is a long-term relationship. If I helped you think through coverage when you were living in Moorpark or Thousand Oaks, it makes no sense for me to hand you off to a stranger the day you load a moving truck.

If you are still on the California side of this move and planning ahead, that is the best time to review your coverage, because your health, your income, and your family obligations may all look different once you are settled in a new state. And if you have already made the move and your policy paperwork still shows a Conejo Valley address, that is worth fixing now rather than leaving it for your beneficiaries to sort out later.
